[[File:01 law isolatedvertex.webm|thumb|Animation showing that the probability that a graph has an isolated vertex goes to 0 when the size of the graph goes to infinity. The property "having an isolated vertex" is almost surely false.]]
In [[mathematical logic]], '''zero-one law''' is a property of a [[logic]] saying that any property is either almost surely true or almost surely false.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Libkin |first=Leonid |date=2004 |title=Elements of Finite Model Theory |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-662-07003-1?error=cookies_not_supported&code=fbdc8b1a-c8e1-4543-80d3-c353fb020b52 |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-07003-1|isbn=978-3-642-05948-3 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Zero-one law holds for [[first-order logic]] (without function symbols<ref name=":1">{{Citation |last=Gurevich |first=Yuri |chapter=Zero-one laws |date=June 1993 |title=Current Trends in Theoretical Computer Science |volume=40 |pages=293–309 |chapter-url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789812794499_0022 |access-date=2026-06-07 |series=World Scientific Series in Computer Science |publisher=World Scientific |doi=10.1142/9789812794499_0022 |isbn=978-981-02-1462-3|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>), first-order logic extended with fixed point operators and first-order with infinite disjunctions and conjunctions. It does not hold for [[Monadic second-order logic|monadic second order logic]].

As pointed out by [[Yuri Gurevich]],<ref name=":1" /> zero-one law was proven for first-order logic by Yu. V. Glebskii, D. I. Kogan, M. I. Liogon'kii & V. A. Talanov <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Glebskii |first1=Yu. V. |last2=Kogan |first2=D. I. |last3=Liogon'kii |first3=M. I. |last4=Talanov |first4=V. A. |date=1969-03-01 |title=Range and degree of realizability of formulas in the restricted predicate calculus |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01071084 |journal=Cybernetics |language=en |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=142–154 |doi=10.1007/BF01071084 |issn=1573-8337|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and independently by [[Ronald Fagin]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fagin |first=Ronald |date=1976 |title=Probabilities on Finite Models |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2272945 |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=50–58 |doi=10.2307/2272945 |jstor=2272945 |issn=0022-4812}}</ref>

== Principle ==
In this article, to keep it simple, we talk about graphs instead of considering arbitrary structures. Given a sentence <math>\varphi</math> in some logic, we define <math>\mu_n(\varphi)</math> to be the proportion of graphs that satisfy <math>\varphi</math> among the graphs with exactly <math>n</math> vertices. We say that a logic has the '''zero-one law''' if <math>\mu_n(\varphi)</math> converges to 1 or 0, for any sentence <math>\varphi</math> of that logic. We set <math>\mu(\varphi)</math> to be that limit to which <math>\mu_n(\varphi)</math> converges when <math>n</math> grows to infinity.

== Examples ==
We give the examples given in <ref name=":0" /> p.&nbsp;236.

=== Even ===
Any logic in which "being of size even" is expressible by a formula  <math>\varphi</math> does not have the zero-one law. Indeed,  <math>\mu_n(\varphi) = 1</math> if <math>n</math> is even and <math>\mu_n(\varphi) = 0</math> if <math>n</math> is odd. And the sequence <math>(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, ...)</math> does not converge.

=== Isolated vertex ===
Consider the first-order formula <math>\varphi</math> that says that there is an isolated vertex: <math>\exists x \forall y \lnot E(x, y)</math>. We have <math>\mu_n(\varphi) \leq \frac{n \cdot 2^{\binom {n-1}2}}{2^{\binom n 2}} = \frac n {2^{n-1}}</math>

Indeed, first <math>2^{\binom {n}2}</math>is the total number of  graphs with exactly <math>n</math> vertices. Second, there are <math>n</math> choices for the isolated vertex, and <math>2^{\binom {n-1}2}</math>ways to put edges on the remaining vertices. Thus, <math>n \cdot 2^{\binom {n-1}2}</math>is an upper bound on the number of graphs with <math>n</math> vertices having an isolated vertex. Thus, <math>\mu(\varphi) = 0</math>.

== First-order logic ==
In this section, we consider first-order logic without function symbols. Note that with function symbols, zero-one law may fail. For instance, the formula <math>p(c)</math>where <math>c</math> is a constant symbol (i.e. a function symbol of arity 0) would be true half of the times.<ref name=":1" />

=== Statement ===
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = First-order logic has the zero-one law: for all first-order formulas <math>\phi</math>, either <math>\mu(\varphi) = 0</math> or <math>\mu(\varphi) = 1</math>.
}}
First-order logic has the zero-one law. The main ingredients of the proof presented in <ref name=":0" /> (their proof is about first-order logic with infinite conjunctions and disjunctions but the idea is similar) are the following.

First we introduce so-called extension axioms. The extension axiom <math>EA_{n, m}</math> says that for any two disjoint subsets <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> of respective cardinality <math>n</math> and  <math>m</math>, there is a point <math>z</math> connected to any points in <math>X</math>, but no points in <math>Y</math>. We show that <math>\mu(EA_{n, m}) = 1</math>.

Second, via pebble games, they prove that if two finite graphs satisfy all the extension axioms <math>EA_{n, m}</math> with <math>n, m \leq k</math>, then they satisfy the same first-order formulas with at most <math>k</math> variables.

=== Decidability ===
[[File:Rado_graph.svg|thumb|The Rado graph which is the model in which true formulas are exactly the formulas <math>\varphi</math> such that <math>\mu(\varphi) = 1</math>]]
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = It is decidable to know whether <math>\mu(\varphi) = 0</math> or <math>\mu(\varphi) = 1</math> for a given first-order formula <math>\phi</math>.
}}
We can define the theory <math>\textbf{EA}</math> of all extension axioms. This theory is <math>\omega</math>-categorial, meaning that it has only one countable model up to isomorphism. It turns out that model is the [[Rado graph]]. Thus, by Lowenheim-Skolem theorem, we can prove that <math>\textbf{EA}</math> is complete, meaning that for any sentence <math>\varphi</math>, either <math>\varphi</math> or <math>\lnot \varphi</math> is entailed by <math>\textbf{EA}</math>. As <math>\textbf{EA}</math> is recursive (we have an algorithm that tells whether a formula is an extension axiom or not), we can decide whether <math>\varphi</math> or <math>\lnot \varphi</math> is entailed by <math>\textbf{EA}</math>, which is equivalent to deciding whether <math>\mu(\varphi) = 1</math> or <math>\mu(\varphi) = 0</math>. Moreover this problem has been shown to be [[PSPACE-complete]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grandjean |first1=Etienne |year=1983 |title=Complexity of the first-order theory of almost all finite structures |journal=Information and Control |volume=57 |issue=2–3 |pages=180–204 |doi=10.1016/S0019-9958(83)80043-6 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Other logics ==
The following logics have the zero-one law:

* First-order logic (as seen above)
* First-order logic <math>L^{\omega}_{\infty \omega}</math> with infinite conjunctions and disjunctions (see Theorem 12.2 in <ref name=":0" />)
* First-order logic with least fixed-point operators, first-order logic with inflationary fixed-point operators, with partial fixed-point operators (see Corollary 12.3 in <ref name=":0" />)
* <math>\exists SO(\exists^*\forall^*)</math> (see Theorem 12.12 in <ref name=":0" />)
* <math>\exists SO(\exists^*\forall\exists^*)</math> (see Theorem 12.15 in <ref name=":0" />)
* First-order logic on grids<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Coupier |first1=David |last2=Desolneux |first2=Agnès |last3=Ycart |first3=Bernard |date=2004 |editor-last=Drmota |editor-first=Michael |title=Mathematics and Computer Science III |chapter=A Zero-One Law for First-Order Logic on Random Images |editor2-last=Flajolet |editor2-first=Philippe |editor3-last=Gardy |editor3-first=Danièle |editor4-last=Gittenberger |editor4-first=Bernhard   |chapter-url=https://hal.science/hal-00020672  |language=en |location=Basel |publisher=Birkhäuser |pages=495–505 |doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-7915-6_48 |isbn=978-3-0348-7915-6}}</ref>

The following logics do not have the zero-one law:

* First-order logic with least fixed-point operators with a predicate < interpreted as a total order on the domain (see second paragraph after Corollary 12.3 in <ref name=":0" />)
* <math>\exists SO(\forall\forall\exists)</math> even if the FO part does not use equality (see Theorem 12.16 in <ref name=":0" />)
* MSO (see Exercice 12.6 in <ref name=":0" />)
* First-order logic with unary function symbols does not have the zero-one law, but has the convergence law, meaning that for all formulas <math>\varphi</math>, the quantity <math>\mu_n(\varphi)</math> converges.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lynch |first=James F. |date=1985 |title=Probabilities of First-Order Sentences about Unary Functions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1999661 |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=287 |issue=2 |pages=543–568 |doi=10.2307/1999661 |jstor=1999661 |issn=0002-9947}}</ref>
